matches.rationale: The finding describes a text-table inconsistency where the text understates the improvement (1-2%) while the table shows large gains (5.7-5.9 pp). The ground truth concerns unrealistically large reported improvements (~5% and >13%) and suspicious consistency across datasets. These are different scientific issues, not the same underlying corruption.
The finding (pred_id 2) refers to Section 4.6 and Table 7, which is unrelated to the method logic inconsistency in the Merging Discriminator and Frustum Culling described in gt_id 2.
No finding addresses the exaggerated novelty claim in the Introduction (Section 1) regarding mask accuracy vs. semantic alignment.
No finding detects the omitted details about data leakage or environment overlap in the pre-exploration and lifelong memory experiments.
No finding mentions the omission of ethical approvals, consent, or safety protocols in the real-world robot experiments.
No finding addresses the inflated rhetorical claim in the Abstract about 'sets new state-of-the-art performance' and 'practical deployment'.
No finding captures the reference misuse and exaggeration of uniqueness in the Related Work section.
No finding references the overreaching claims in the Conclusion about strong generalization and state-of-the-art results, which contradict earlier cautious statements.

Both address the missing or inconsistent ablation of 3D representation quality degradation in the noise robustness experiments (Section 4.6, Table 7). The finding points out a text-table inconsistency where the text claims feature dropout and spatial jitter ablations, but the table lacks them, which directly reflects the ground truth's concern that robustness to 3D representation quality was not properly explored.
No finding covers the missing ethical statements about data consent and privacy in the Appendix (Section A.1).
No finding discusses the unsupported claim about balancing real-time adaptability with long-term memory, missing metrics on memory saturation or forgetting.
No finding addresses the absolute, unqualified claim of state-of-the-art performance in the Introduction's contribution list.
